title: Class 3 — AI-Assisted Single-Cell and Spatial Analysis
text:
In single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, a single experiment can generate expression profiles for hundreds of thousands of cells, dozens of cell types, and thousands of genes, spread across multiple conditions, tissues, and time points. Making sense of this volume of information (data processing, annotating cell types, inferring cell–cell communication, integrating multiple omics layers) or simply keeping up with the literature, has increasingly become a bottleneck that outpaces what a single researcher can process manually.
Artificial intelligence, and more specifically large language models (LLMs), have entered this space from two directions at once. On one side, purpose-built generative models trained directly on single-cell and spatial data (e.g., scGPT, deepGPS, MIDAS, MultiVI, SpatialScope, DeepTalk) are being used to annotate cell types, impute missing values, integrate modalities, and infer spatial gene expression at resolutions that were previously unreachable (Simizo et al., 2026). On the other side, general-purpose conversational LLMs such as ChatGPT are being adopted as everyday assistants for coding, data cleaning, writing, and even hypothesis generation in computational biology labs (Lubiana et al., 2023).



Range of AI applications in cell biology (source: Simizo et al., 2026).


This course is concerned with both fronts, but this introduction focuses on setting the stage: what LLMs can realistically do for you in this domain, what they cannot be trusted to do, and how to use them so that the “goods” outweigh the “bads.”





Deep learning and generative AI approaches have transformed several stages of the single-cell and spatial transcriptomics pipeline:

Cell type annotation and clustering — models like scGPT (Cui et al., 2024) and scGNN (Wang et al., 2021) use transformer or graph-based architectures to annotate cell types and impute gene expression with performance that often exceeds classical pipelines.
Multi-omics integration — frameworks such as MIDAS (He et al., 2024) and MultiVI (Ashuach et al., 2023) combine RNA, ATAC, and protein data from different technologies into a single coherent representation, something that is extremely laborious to do by hand.
Spatial context — tools like SpatialScope (Wan et al., 2023) and DeepTalk (Yang et al., 2024) infer transcriptome-wide expression at single-cell resolution from spatial data and reconstruct ligand–receptor interactions, directly supporting the kind of tissue-architecture questions this course addresses.




Independently of domain-specific models, general-purpose LLMs like Claude and ChatGPT have proven useful for the day-to-day mechanics of computational biology work: making code more readable, writing documentation, generating regular expressions to clean messy metadata, drafting analysis code, improving figures, and helping with academic writing, especially for non-native English speakers. None of this replaces domain expertise, but it removes friction from tasks that otherwise consume a disproportionate share of a researcher’s time.



Perhaps the most interesting (and most debated) use case is hypothesis generation. Frameworks such as FieldSHIFT (O’Brien et al., 2024) use in-context learning to propose candidate research directions by finding analogies across scientific domains, and although their unsupervised success rate is still well below that of human experts, a meaningful fraction of the generated hypotheses have been validated by follow-up analysis (Simizo et al., 2026). This illustrates a useful way to think about LLMs in research: not as oracles that produce ready-made answers, but as idea amplifiers — tools that broaden the space of hypotheses a researcher considers, provided that every suggestion is still filtered through domain knowledge and, ideally, experimental or computational validation before it is taken seriously.






The single most important limitation to internalize before using any LLM in research is hallucination: the model can generate fluent, confident, and completely fabricated content — nonexistent functions or libraries, invented citations, plausible-sounding but wrong biological claims. This is not a rare edge case; it is a structural property of how these models generate text, and it applies as much to code as to biological reasoning (Lubiana et al., 2023). In a computational biology context this is particularly dangerous because a hallucinated function call or an invented parameter may run without error yet silently corrupt downstream results.



Even when a model is not hallucinating, its outputs are frequently difficult to interpret. Most deep learning systems used in cell biology (including LLM-based ones) operate as “black boxes,” which complicates biological validation, bias detection, and — critically for translational work — regulatory approval and clinical adoption (Simizo et al., 2026). Explainable AI (XAI) techniques such as SHAP, LIME, Grad-CAM++, and attention-based architectures are being developed specifically to address this gap, but interpretability remains an open problem rather than a solved one.



Model performance depends heavily on the quality and representativeness of training data. Batch effects, technical noise, and — especially relevant globally — the underrepresentation of non-European ancestries in single-cell and spatial genomics datasets can bake bias directly into model predictions, an issue that recent Latin American initiatives are explicitly trying to counter by building more inclusive datasets (Simizo et al., 2026).



Finally, there is a human-side risk: overreliance. If a lab becomes dependent on a single external tool for tasks that used to require (and build) in-house expertise, it becomes vulnerable to outages, price changes, or access restrictions, and risks eroding fundamental skills in its trainees. This has practical consequences that go beyond productivity — the same critical thinking needed to catch a hallucinated function is what erodes if it is never exercised (Lubiana et al., 2023).




The papers underlying this course converge on a similar message: LLMs are worth adopting, but only within a disciplined workflow. A few concrete practices to carry into this course:

Never trust, always verify. Treat any LLM-generated code, citation, or biological claim as a draft that must be checked against documentation, the literature, or an independent computational test — you remain responsible for anything you publish, not the model.
Only ask for what you can evaluate. Use LLMs to help with syntax or concepts you already understand well enough to test; this limits the damage of undetected hallucinations, especially for beginners.
Invest in prompt design. Vague prompts produce vague, unfocused answers; specifying context, the exact task, and the desired output format substantially improves reliability.
Prefer domain-specific models for domain-specific tasks. For single-cell and spatial transcriptomics specifically, purpose-trained tools (scGPT, SpatialScope, DeepTalk, MIDAS, MultiVI, etc.) are generally more trustworthy for quantitative analysis than a general-purpose chatbot, which is better suited to code support, writing, and brainstorming (Simizo et al., 2026).
Use LLMs to widen, not replace, your hypothesis space. Let them suggest candidate directions or analogies, then subject each candidate to the same scrutiny you would apply to a hypothesis proposed by a colleague.
Keep humans and human interaction in the loop. Preserve practices like code review, pair programming, and lab discussionsç. These remain the best defense against both technical errors and the erosion of expertise.

title: Welcome!
text:
Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics are transforming how we study biology. Traditional approaches often measure gene expression across large populations of cells, which can hide important differences between individual cells. In contrast, single-cell technologies allow us to explore individual cells and their molecular states, while spatial transcriptomics adds another layer by showing where those cells are located and how they are organized within tissues.



From the “smoothie” to the individual ingredients and where they are in the tissue. Bulk RNA sequencing provides an average molecular profile across many cells, while single-cell transcriptomics allows us to distinguish individual cellular populations. Spatial omics goes one step further by revealing where these cells and molecular signals are located within the tissue.





From bulk RNA-seq to analyzing individual cells expression profiles and understanding the microenvironment. (source https://www.cas.org/resources/cas-insights/spatial-transcriptomics).


Therefore, these technologies open the door to questions that were previously difficult or impossible to answer. Which immune cells are present in a tissue, and how do their states change during inflammation? Which cells are producing inflammatory signals, and which cells are responding to them? How do immune cells interact with epithelial, stromal, or other tissue cells? And where do these interactions occur within the tissue?
At the same time, working with single-cell and spatial data can feel overwhelming at first. Datasets can be large and complex, terminology can be unfamiliar, and analyses often involve specialized computational tools or programming skills. This course is designed to make these technologies more approachable. We will start by exploring user-friendly tools that allow you to interact with single-cell and spatial data without writing code. We will then move into reproducible analysis with R and Python, before exploring how AI can help us write, test, and improve analytical workflows.


Before we start exploring the tools and analyses, let’s take a moment to understand what single-cell and spatial transcriptomics actually measure and why they are so useful.


In a traditional bulk RNA-seq experiment, RNA is collected from a large population of cells and measured together. The resulting expression profile represents an average across all of those cells. This can be useful, but it can also hide important biological differences. Imagine a tissue containing immune cells, epithelial cells, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells. If all of their RNA is mixed together, we can see which genes are expressed in the tissue overall—but we may not know which cells are expressing those genes. Single-cell transcriptomics changes this by separating the sample into individual cells—or, more precisely, individual cell-derived measurements—and profiling their gene expression separately.
Instead of asking:

What genes are expressed in this tissue?

we can begin to ask:

Which cells are present, what are they expressing, and how do their molecular states differ?

This is particularly powerful for studying immune responses and inflammation. A tissue that appears to have a strong inflammatory response may contain several different immune populations, each with distinct roles. Single-cell data can help us distinguish these populations and explore their molecular states—for example, identifying activated macrophages, different T-cell states, or inflammatory signaling programs.



Single-cell transcriptomics gives us detailed information about what cells are doing, but in many experiments we lose an important piece of information: where those cells were located within the tissue. This spatial context is particularly important when studying inflammation, where cellular behavior is strongly influenced by the local microenvironment. Immune cells, stromal cells, epithelial cells, and other cell types can occupy distinct tissue niches and interact with one another through localized signaling, cell–cell contacts, and gradients of cytokines and other molecular factors. Knowing where cells are located therefore allows us to understand not only which genes and pathways are active, but also where inflammatory processes are occurring and how neighboring cells contribute to or respond to them. Preserving spatial information can reveal localized molecular processes, identify inflammatory niches, and help uncover interactions between different cell populations that may be missed when tissue architecture is lost. Spatial transcriptomics addresses this by measuring gene expression while preserving information about its spatial location.
This allows us to ask questions such as:

Where are inflammatory cells located?


Which regions of a tissue show inflammatory activity?


Are immune cells located close to the cells they may be interacting with?


Do particular cellular states occur in specific tissue structures or microenvironments?

In other words, spatial transcriptomics allows us to connect molecular identity with tissue organization.



Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics therefore provide complementary perspectives:

Single-cell: Who is there, and what are they doing?
Spatial: Where are they, and what is happening around them?

Together, these technologies allow us to move beyond simply describing which genes are expressed. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics approaches provide complementary perspectives on tissue biology: single-cell methods can provide high-resolution characterization of individual cell populations and their transcriptional states, while spatial methods preserve information about where those cells and molecular programs are located within the tissue. Importantly, not all spatial transcriptomic technologies resolve individual cells, and different approaches vary in their spatial resolution, molecular detection strategies, and whether they rely on targeted, probe-based measurements or untargeted sequencing. By integrating these complementary views, we can begin to understand which cells are involved, how their states change, how they communicate, and where these processes occur within a tissue. This is particularly valuable in inflammation, where cellular states and molecular interactions are often shaped by their local microenvironment and spatial organization.

Critically evaluate computational and biological suggestions generated by AI.

Most importantly, we hope you leave the course feeling that single-cell and spatial transcriptomics are approachable tools rather than a black box.

2. The main families










Sequencing based (seq-based)
Imaging based (in situ)
Region based (ROI)




Principle
Slide carries oligos with a known positional barcode. mRNA diffuses, is captured, sequenced, and position is recovered from the barcode
Fluorescent probes hybridize to transcripts inside intact tissue. Each gene gets a color code over successive rounds
User selects regions on the image; only those are collected and sequenced


Genes
Untargeted, whole transcriptome
Targeted, closed panel
Whole transcriptome or panels


Strength
Discovery without prior hypothesis
Subcellular resolution, high sensitivity
Good for defined anatomical regions


Intrinsic limit
Poly-A capture and lateral diffusion limit resolution and sensitivity
You must know the genes beforehand
No continuous map


Examples
Visium, Visium HD, Slide-seq, Stereo-seq
Xenium, CosMx, MERSCOPE, seqFISH, STARmap
GeoMx DSP, LCM-seq, Tomo-seq



Imaging based has two subfamilies: multiplexed ISH (MERFISH, seqFISH, Xenium, CosMx, MERSCOPE) and ISS, in situ sequencing (STARmap, BaristaSeq, HybISS), where the transcript is sequenced on the slide.

title: Class 2 — Reproducible Single-Cell and Spatial Analysis with R and Python
text:
4. Advantages and limitations









Seq-based
Imaging based




Advantages
Whole transcriptome, discovery. Detects unexpected genes. Workflow close to scRNA-seq. Low cost per gene. Visium has the largest user base and most validated tools
True subcellular resolution. High sensitivity. Real per cell data (niches and contacts without deconvolution). Keeps morphology, integrates with H&E and IF. Works well with FFPE and degraded RNA


Limitations
Spots mix cells, rare types get diluted. Needs deconvolution with a scRNA-seq reference. Low capture efficiency, sparse matrices. Poly-A only. Lateral diffusion blurs position. Permeabilization must be tuned per tissue. Small fixed area. High cost per sample. In Visium HD and Stereo-seq the bin is not a cell
Closed panel, no discovery outside it. Segmentation is the main bottleneck: errors create chimeric profiles and false cell types. Optical crowding of abundant genes. Autofluorescence (lipofuscin, collagen, red blood cells). Huge data (hundreds of GB to TB). Long instrument time, high cost. Less mature analysis ecosystem

title: Class 2 — Reproducible Single-Cell and Spatial Analysis with R and Python
section: 7. Single-cell vs. spatial: preprocessing and cell annotation
text:
7. Single-cell vs. spatial: preprocessing and cell annotation
Both fields share the same conceptual pipeline — QC, normalization, dimensionality reduction, clustering, annotation. The difference is not the list of steps, it is what a row of the count matrix actually represents.
In scRNA-seq the cell is defined by the chemistry itself: the tissue is dissociated, one cell goes into one droplet, and every transcript in that droplet is by construction assigned to that cell. In spatial data the cell is never given. It has to be reconstructed computationally, and the way it is reconstructed depends entirely on the technology family.

7.1 What the measurement unit is








Technology family
Unit in the matrix
Relation to a cell




scRNA-seq / snRNA-seq
Droplet or well
One cell (barring doublets and empty droplets)


Spot-based (Visium, original ST, Slide-seq)
Spot or bead
Fixed capture area. A 55 µm Visium spot typically pools ~1 to 10 cells of mixed types. The cell does not exist in the data


High-resolution seq-based (Visium HD, Stereo-seq, Seq-Scope)
Bin (arbitrary square, e.g. 2, 8 or 16 µm)
A bin is a grid square, not a biological object. It may cut one cell across several bins, or pool fragments of neighbors


Imaging-based (Xenium, CosMx, MERSCOPE)
Segmented cell
Raw data is a point cloud of individual transcripts with (x, y) coordinates. A “cell” only exists after segmentation draws a boundary around a group of those points


Region-based (GeoMx, LCM)
User-drawn ROI
Whatever the user selected. No single-cell claim at all




The consequence: in spot- and bin-based data the analytical problem is mixture (which cell types compose this unit, and in what proportion). In imaging-based data the problem is assignment (which cell does this transcript belong to). These are different problems and they need different tools.



7.2 Preprocessing, step by step








Step
scRNA-seq
Spatial




QC metrics
Counts per cell, genes per cell, % mitochondrial, doublet score
Same metrics, but the thresholds mean something different. A low-count Visium spot may be a genuinely sparse tissue region, not a dying cell. In imaging-based data, counts per cell scale with the panel size (a 300-gene panel gives far fewer counts than a whole transcriptome) and with cell area, so a “low-count” cell may simply be a small lymphocyte


% mitochondrial
Standard proxy for dying cells
Often unusable: mitochondrial genes are frequently absent from targeted panels, and in FFPE the metric is not interpretable the same way. Needs different QC proxies


Doublet detection
Core step (Scrublet, DoubletFinder)
Meaningless in spot/bin data — every spot is a “multiplet” by design; the problem is handled by deconvolution instead. In imaging-based data, “doublets” are not chemistry artifacts but segmentation errors (two cells merged into one), which is a different failure mode and needs different diagnostics


Ambient RNA
Free-floating RNA in the droplet suspension (SoupX, CellBender)
The analogous problem is transcript spillover / lateral diffusion: RNA that physically drifted away from its cell of origin, or extracellular transcripts sitting between cells. Imaging platforms include negative control probes (blank codewords) to estimate the false-detection rate directly


Segmentation
Not applicable — cells are already physically separated
The central preprocessing step for imaging-based data. See 7.3


Deconvolution
Not applicable
Required for spot-based data to estimate cell-type proportions per spot (RCTD, Cell2location, SPOTlight, Stereoscope, cell2location)


Normalization
Library size + log, or SCTransform
Same formulas, but total counts per unit confound with cell/spot area and local tissue density, not only with capture efficiency. A dense lymphoid region will have higher counts per spot than sparse stroma for purely anatomical reasons — this is biology-driven, not technical, and normalizing it away can erase real signal


Batch / slide effects
Between samples and chemistries
Also between slides, capture areas and fields of view (FOVs) within the same experiment. FOV-edge artifacts are a known imaging-platform issue


Spatial-specific QC
None
Detecting which spots are actually under tissue, alignment/registration to the H&E or IF image, checking panel coverage for the cell types of interest, and inspecting the image itself for folds, tears and detachment





7.3 Why segmentation is the problem in imaging-based data
The raw data contains no cells. A Xenium or CosMx run outputs a list of decoded transcripts, each with a gene identity and an (x, y) — often (x, y, z) — coordinate. Nothing in that file says which transcript came from which cell. Building the count matrix means drawing boundaries on the image and summing the transcripts that fall inside each boundary. Everything downstream is therefore conditional on the quality of the cell-boundary detection. If the boundary is wrong, the expression profile is wrong, and no amount of clustering, normalization or annotation will recover it.
How the errors manifest








Error
Mechanism
Downstream consequence




False merge
Two adjacent cells enclosed in one boundary
A chimeric profile: a T cell fused with an epithelial cell produces a unit expressing both CD3E and EPCAM. It clusters separately and is easily mistaken for a novel “intermediate” or “transitional” cell state


False split
One cell divided into two units
Halves the counts, dilutes markers, creates artificially low-quality cells that get discarded by QC — biasing against large or irregularly shaped cell types


Transcript spillover
Transcripts of cell A assigned to cell B
The most insidious error: it does not look broken. Highly expressed genes from an abundant neighbor bleed into every surrounding cell, generating false co-expression and inflating apparent cell-cell “interaction” signal


Orphan transcripts
Real transcripts with no assignable cell (e.g. the nucleus lies outside the section plane)
Lost signal, systematically biased toward cell types with large or elongated morphology



The critical point is that these errors are indistinguishable from biology after the fact. A chimeric merged cell looks exactly like a real hybrid cell state. Spillover looks exactly like a real ligand-receptor neighborhood. This is why segmentation must be inspected on the image, not merely accepted as a preprocessing default.
Why nucleus expansion and Voronoi tessellation are weak solutions
Both are geometric shortcuts used because the nuclear stain (DAPI) is trivially easy to segment while the cell boundary is not. Both replace a biological boundary with a mathematical one.
Fixed-radius nucleus expansion — segment nuclei, then dilate each by a constant distance (commonly 5–15 µm) and call that the cell:

It assumes every cell has the same size and shape. A resting lymphocyte (~7 µm) and a macrophage, tumor cell or neuron (30 µm and up, with processes) get the same treatment. Small cells are over-expanded into their neighbors; large cells are truncated, losing most of their cytoplasmic transcripts.
Most mRNA is cytoplasmic, and cytoplasmic geometry is exactly what the nuclear stain does not tell you. Polarized epithelium, elongated fibroblasts, dendritic processes and neuronal projections are all badly approximated by a disc.
It fails hardest precisely where the biology is most interesting: densely packed tissue (lymph node, germinal centre, tumor nest), where every expansion necessarily crosses into a neighbor.

Voronoi / Delaunay tessellation — partition the plane so each point belongs to the nearest nucleus:

It partitions all available space, so every transcript is assigned to some cell. There is no “unassigned”, no extracellular compartment, no acellular matrix. Ambient and extracellular transcripts are forced into cells by construction.
It produces convex polygons that tile the plane, which no real tissue does. Non-convex, interdigitating and wrapping morphologies (podocytes, astrocytes, dendritic cells) cannot be represented.
Cells whose nucleus is outside the plane of section have no seed at all, so their territory is silently absorbed by neighbors — a 2D slice through a 3D tissue guarantees this happens.

The shared failure of both: they use only nuclear position, ignoring the transcript distribution itself and any real membrane information.
What actually improves segmentation







Strategy
What it adds




Membrane and boundary protein staining
The direct fix: image the actual cell border. Xenium’s multi-tissue stain (e.g. ATP1A1, E-cadherin, CD45) and CosMx’s morphology markers (PanCK, CD45, CD298/B2M, membrane markers) provide channels that mark membranes and compartments, so the boundary is measured rather than assumed. Choosing markers that cover your cell types matters — a panel with only epithelial and immune boundary markers will still segment stroma poorly


Deep-learning segmentation on those channels
Cellpose, StarDist, Mesmer/DeepCell learn irregular, non-convex shapes from image data instead of imposing a disc or polygon. Only as good as the input stains, and usually benefits from tissue-specific fine-tuning


Transcript-aware / probabilistic segmentation
Baysor, ClusterMap, JSTA, BIDCell, proseg use the transcript point cloud itself as evidence: transcripts with coherent expression identity are grouped together, boundaries follow molecular composition rather than geometry alone, and — crucially — transcripts can be left unassigned instead of being forced into a cell. Combining these with a membrane-stain prior generally outperforms either alone


3D / multi-plane imaging
Reduces the orphan-nucleus problem caused by sectioning 3D cells into a 2D plane


Post-hoc segmentation QC
Check for biologically impossible co-expression (CD3E with EPCAM, PTPRC with KRT), inspect the fraction of unassigned transcripts, compare counts-per-cell against cell area, and re-run with a second segmentation method to see which conclusions survive. If a “novel cell state” disappears under a different segmentation, it was an artifact


Segmentation-free analysis
For some questions (spatial domains, gene co-localization, tissue niches) the cell is not required at all — analysing the transcript point cloud or binned data directly avoids the error entirely




Practical rule: never accept the vendor’s default segmentation without looking at it overlaid on the image, and treat any surprising “hybrid” cell type as a segmentation artifact until proven otherwise.



7.4 Cell type annotation








Aspect
scRNA-seq
Spatial




Starting point
A real single cell with whole-transcriptome coverage. Marker-based or reference-based annotation applies directly
Depends on family. Spot-based: the unit is a mixture, so the question shifts from “which type is this?” to “which types compose this, in what proportion?”. Imaging-based: the unit is a reconstructed cell, and annotation is only as trustworthy as its boundary


Method
Marker scoring, or label transfer from a reference (SingleR, Azimuth, scANVI, CellTypist)
Spot-based: deconvolution against a matched scRNA-seq reference (RCTD, Cell2location, SPOTlight). Imaging-based: same label-transfer logic as scRNA-seq, restricted to the panel genes


Reference dependency
Helpful, not mandatory
For spot-based, effectively mandatory — and the reference must match the tissue, condition and species. A mismatched reference will confidently assign cell types that are not there


Gene coverage
~20,000 genes; any marker is available
Imaging platforms use a closed panel of a few hundred to a few thousand genes. If the markers distinguishing two subtypes were not designed into the panel, those subtypes are unresolvable, permanently. Panel design is therefore an annotation decision made before the experiment runs


Achievable granularity
Fine-grained states (e.g. Tem vs Trm vs exhausted CD8)
Spot-based: broad classes only; rare types get diluted below detection. Imaging-based: close to scRNA-seq granularity if the panel and segmentation cooperate — in practice, coarse labels are far more defensible than fine states


Output
One label per cell
Spot-based: a proportion vector per spot. Imaging-based: one label per segmented cell, plus a large fraction of low-count cells that resist confident labelling


Validation
Marker expression, known biology, reference agreement
All of the above plus spatial coherence, which is a genuinely independent check: annotated epithelium should line the lumen, germinal-centre B cells should form follicles, endothelium should trace vessels. Labels that are anatomically scattered are usually wrong


Additional analyses unlocked
None — position is destroyed at dissociation
Spatial domains, cellular niches and neighbourhoods, distance-to-structure analyses, and spatially constrained ligand-receptor inference




Bottom line: scRNA-seq annotation is essentially “which reference, which markers”. Spatial annotation carries a prior question that must be answered first — “do I even trust my unit of measurement?” For spot-based data that means asking how much cell-type mixing sits inside each spot; for imaging-based data it means asking how good the segmentation is. Skipping that question does not remove the error, it just makes it invisible.
